original_question: A 20-year-old male comes into your office two days after falling during a pick up basketball game. The patient states that the lateral aspect of his knee collided with another player's knee. On exam, the patient's right knee appears the same size as his left knee without any swelling or effusion. The patient has intact sensation and strength in both lower extremities. The patient's right knee has no laxity upon varus stress test, but is more lax upon valgus stress test when compared to his left knee. Lachman's test and posterior drawer test both have firm endpoints without laxity. Which of the following structures has this patient injured?

base.stage_1: A 20-year-old male presents to the office complaining of right knee pain after a basketball injury two days ago.
base.stage_2: The patient reports that the lateral aspect of his right knee collided with another player's knee during a pickup basketball game. On examination, the right knee appears to be the same size as the left, with no visible swelling or effusion. Sensation and strength are intact bilaterally in the lower extremities. Varus stress test is negative, but valgus stress test demonstrates laxity compared to the contralateral knee. Lachman's and posterior drawer tests are negative with firm endpoints.
base.stage_3: An MRI of the right knee demonstrates hyperintensity along the medial collateral ligament without disruption of the anterior cruciate ligament, posterior cruciate ligament, or lateral collateral ligament.
base.stage_4: Orthopedic consultation confirms the diagnosis of a grade II medial collateral ligament sprain based on exam findings and MRI results. Conservative management with bracing and physical therapy is recommended.

counterfactuals.alteration_description: The presence of a large effusion argues against an isolated MCL injury, which typically presents with minimal to no effusion.
